lead: Load a ruler held out over the edge of a table and it dips. A beam bends the same way: the upper face stretches, the lower face compresses, and one thin layer in between keeps its length — the neutral surface. The resisting moment depends on the material through Y and on the shape through I, the second moment of area. That one relation, M = YI/R, fixes how far any beam sags. Engineers size bridge girders, balcony slabs and crane jibs with it, and a wrong depth turns a 5 mm sag into 50 mm. Only a few universities teach it as a full chapter.
prereq: You need: 1.2 Elasticity — stress, strain and Young's modulus Y, the material constant that appears in every formula here.

sections.h3: Neutral surface and the bending moment

blocks.text: Bend a straight beam into an arc of radius R. Fibres on the outer side lengthen, fibres on the inner side shorten, and one surface in between neither lengthens nor shortens: the neutral surface. Its line across any cross-section is the neutral axis. A fibre at distance y from that axis carries strain y/R, so its stress is Yy/R, with Y the Young's modulus in Pa.

Those stresses act on every element of area, and their moments about the neutral axis add to the bending moment M at that section. The sum is (Y/R)∫y² dA, and that integral is the second moment of area I. So the moment a section can carry and the curvature it takes are locked together.

blocks.where: M is the bending moment in N m, the couple the loads produce at that section; Y is Young's modulus in Pa; I is the second moment of area about the neutral axis, in m⁴; R is the radius of curvature in m. A large YI means a large R, that is, gentle bending.
b is the breadth in m; d is the depth in m, measured along the load — the dimension that bends; r is the radius of a circular section in m.

blocks.text: A cantilever is clamped at one end and free at the other. Hang a load W (newtons) at the free end. At distance x from the clamp, the load to the right of that section makes a moment M = W(L − x), where L is the length in m. For small sags the curvature 1/R is d²y/dx². Integrating twice, with zero slope and zero sag at the clamp, gives the free-end sag.

blocks.where: δ is the free-end sag in m; W is the end load in N; L is the cantilever length in m; the second form uses I = bd³/12 for a rectangular strip of breadth b and depth d, both in m. Twice the depth sags eight times less, because of the d³.

blocks.text: Now rest a beam on two knife edges a distance l apart and hang W at the middle. Symmetry makes the slope zero at the centre, and the sag there is δ = Wl³/(4Ybd³). Rearranged, Y = Wl³/(4bd³δ) — the non-uniform bending experiment. Measure δ with a pin and a travelling microscope. Apply a pure couple at both ends instead and the curvature is the same everywhere; some syllabi call that uniform bending and run it as a separate experiment.

Each element of area contributes A y² to I, so area far from the neutral axis earns far more resistance than area near it. An I-section puts two heavy flanges at the top and bottom and joins them with a thin web that mainly holds them apart. Mass sits where it works hardest. Railway bridge girders and crane jibs use this I-shape directly; a roof truss gets the same benefit by separating a top chord and a bottom chord with a light web of members.

figure.caption: A 4.9 N tip load makes a bending moment; M = YI/R turns that moment into curvature; integrating the curvature along the 0.50 m length gives a 4.9 mm sag at the free end.

spec.title: From load to sag
spec.aria: Four steps: a 4.9 N tip load creates a bending moment, the term YI/R fixes the curvature, and integrating over the 0.50 m length gives a free-end sag of 4.9 mm.

examples.question: A steel cantilever 0.50 m long, 20 mm wide and 5.0 mm thick carries a 0.50 kg load at its free end. Take Y = 2.0×10¹¹ Pa and g = 9.8 m/s². Find the second moment of area I about the neutral axis and the sag δ of the free end.
steps: Convert to metres: L = 0.50 m, b = 0.020 m, d = 0.0050 m. The thickness 5.0 mm is the depth, because the load bends the strip across that dimension.
examples.answer: I = 2.08×10⁻¹⁰ m⁴ and the free end sags δ = 4.9×10⁻³ m, that is 4.9 mm.
examples.check: b = 0.020; d = 0.0050; L = 0.50; m = 0.50; Y = 2.0e11; g = 9.8; I = b*d**3/12; W = m*g; delta = W*L**3/(3*Y*I); print(round(I, 12)); print(round(3*Y*I, 1)); print(round(W, 1)); print(round(delta, 6))

traps: In I = bd³/12 the cube sits on the dimension parallel to the load — the strip's thickness, not its breadth. Swapping b and d changes I by (b/d)².
L must be in metres, like I. A length left in mm makes L³ wrong by 10⁹.
Cantilever has the 3 (δ = WL³/3YI); the centre-loaded beam has the 4 (δ = Wl³/4Ybd³). Examiners love this swap.
In Y = Wl³/(4bd³δ), l is the distance between the knife edges, not the full length of a beam that overhangs them.
All these formulas assume small sag, δ much smaller than L. A strip bent into a semicircle is a different, non-linear problem.

quiz.q: Define the neutral surface and the neutral axis of a bent beam.
quiz.a: The neutral surface is the layer inside a bent beam whose length does not change; its trace on a cross-section is the neutral axis, and distances y are measured from it.

quiz.q: Why does doubling the depth of a rectangular strip reduce the sag eight times, while doubling the breadth only halves it?
quiz.a: δ = 4WL³/(Ybd³). Breadth enters to the first power, so doubling b halves δ. Depth enters as d³ because a deeper strip has more area AND that area sits farther from the neutral axis, so I grows eightfold.

quiz.q: A cantilever has L = 0.40 m, b = 10 mm, d = 2.0 mm and carries W = 2.0 N. Take Y = 2.0×10¹¹ Pa. Find the free-end sag δ.
A steel beam rests on knife edges 1.0 m apart, breadth 20 mm, depth 5.0 mm. A 1.0 kg load at the middle makes the centre sag 4.9 mm. Find Y.
In the pin-and-microscope experiment the load is hung at the centre of the span, not near one support. Why?
quiz.a: At the centre the slope is zero by symmetry, so the sag formula Wl³/(4bd³) holds cleanly and the sag is largest, giving the smallest percentage error in reading δ with the microscope.

quiz.q: Two girders have the same mass and length; one is a solid rectangle, the other an I-section. Why does the I-section sag less?
quiz.a: For the same load and span, the sag scales as δ ∝ 1/I. I = Σ A y², so the I-section puts more area into flanges far from the neutral axis and has the larger I; hence it sags less. Use δ = WL³/(3YI) only for the cantilever case.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real structures are checked with finite-element software that solves the same M = YI/R relation over thousands of small elements. Beam theory here is the Euler–Bernoulli case: sections stay flat and shear is ignored, which fails for short, deep beams. Search for beam deflection boundary conditions, section modulus, and built-up girders if you go into civil or mechanical design. Composite and aluminium bridge decks are an active research area, chosen when a low mass with high YI matters.
